html:
In 1763 Catherine the Great, herself German born, issued a manifesto inviting foreigners to settle in Russia. Thousands of German farmers answered and founded colonies on the lower Volga around Saratov.

She promised them free land, freedom of religion, their own local government, years without taxes, and freedom from army service. Most came from Hesse and the Rhineland, which had been wrecked by the Seven Years' War. In the 1760s about a hundred villages were founded on the open steppe. Life was hard at first, and nomad raids and poor harvests killed many.

The colonies grew and kept their language, Lutheran and Catholic churches and customs. When Russia ended their exemption from army service in 1874, many moved to the United States, Canada, Brazil and Argentina. Under Soviet rule they had their own republic from 1924, but in 1941 Stalin deported them all to Siberia and Kazakhstan.
sum: In 1763 Catherine the Great, herself German born, issued a manifesto inviting foreigners to settle in Russia. Thousands of German farmers answered and founded colonies on the lower Volga around Saratov.
